blocks.text: What the supplied examples teach us about PHVS

These examples provide methods for testing a thesis. Their clinical conclusions and numerical assumptions do not become evidence about Pharvaris. The PHAT deck and workbook concern Phathom Pharmaceuticals, a different company. I inspected the supplied material and traced selected formulas without changing the originals or recalculating the workbook. The other companies’ underlying clinical sources were not independently audited in this review.
PHAT: a smaller market can still support a better business

The PHAT pitch accepts an important bear argument: patients whose symptoms persist on a proton-pump inhibitor do not all have acid-driven disease that stronger acid suppression can treat. It then proposes another source of upside: gastroenterologists may select more suitable patients and generate more repeat use. Slides 9–11 therefore separate eligible population from revenue per treated patient. This is useful for PHVS: determine who needs an oral treatment, how often they use it, whether they continue, and what the manufacturer receives after discounts. A large disease population or strong trial result cannot answer those commercial questions by itself. [X1]

The workbook makes the proposed driver concrete. SUM!F36 holds 80% “capture / adherence”; OpModel!K71 links to it. K72 assumes 150 doses per year, K67 holds 30 doses per bottle, and K74 divides these to produce five potential bottles. K73 multiplies those five bottles by modeled patients in K63 and the 80% factor, implying four realized bottles per patient-year. The corresponding NERD calculation appears in rows 104–107. Holding other inputs fixed, raising capture from 70% to 80% increases these forecast volumes by 80/70−1, or 14.3%. That is a model sensitivity, not proof of an improvement in persistence. [X2]

Slide 10 supports its assumption using correct administration timing, one-year PPI persistence by disease severity, aggregate refill share and physician anecdotes. These are different measures. Refill share can rise when new starts slow, without any improvement in individual retention. For PHVS, use patient cohorts and defined follow-up periods where available; keep prescriber selection, paid starts, continued use and dose frequency separate. [X1]

Two formula problems also show why we should audit an attractive example before copying it. DCF!G37 links to SUM!F21, which links straight back to DCF!G37: the discount rate is circular, while the separately calculated WACC in DCF!G34 does not feed discounting. OpModel!J14 and K14 back-solve gross-to-net discounts by adding H. pylori packs and pack price, rather than multiplying them as the revenue formula does. The latter mixes incompatible units and also feeds the next forecast year through L14. These issues require reconciliation before using the workbook’s precise valuation. [X2]
M Loses Capital: apply the skepticism symmetrically

Parts 2 and 3 provide a useful checklist: examine incentives, distinguish a biological marker from an outcome patients value, interrogate endpoints and ask whether sufficient drug reaches its target for long enough. Apply those questions to management, competitors and bearish commentary alike. Interested statements deserve corroboration, not automatic dismissal. A failure rate across all drugs entering development is also the wrong starting probability for a late-stage program with relevant human evidence. Update the prior for stage, target validation, formulation and trial quality. [X3, X4]

The TTRX article usefully examines an active ointment vehicle, baseline imbalance, changes in endpoints and selection of a subgroup after results were known. Those checks transfer directly to PHVS. But nonsignificance does not establish absence of benefit, and an eleven-patient study of another intervention cannot set a hard ceiling on an entire mechanism. A promising subgroup should generate a prospectively testable hypothesis; it should not inherit the certainty of a replicated randomized result. [X5]

ZURA illustrates the danger of an appealing biological explanation becoming an unsupported numerical forecast. Its assumed mixture, 0.33 × subgroup response + 0.67 × 38.3% = 51.6%, implies roughly 79% response in the proposed subgroup. Yet an assumed 50% subgroup share implies about 65%; equal 51.6% responses in both groups also reproduce the aggregate. Without observing subgroup membership and outcomes, the mechanism is underidentified. Using the supplied counts, 16/31 versus 23/60, the difference is 13.3 percentage points, with an approximate unadjusted 95% interval of −8.2 to +34.7 points. This arithmetic neither reproduces the trial’s Bayesian analysis nor proves subgroup efficacy. Withdrawals also need documented reasons before being classified as nonresponse. [X6]

SLGL supplies the right exposure question: does an ordinary topical formulation deliver enough active drug to the tissue where disease develops? Similar molecular properties are a reason to investigate, not proof that two formulations have identical delivery. A concentration below assay detection is not demonstrated biological zero. For PHVS, the corresponding discipline is to require evidence for the actual formulation, dose and intended use, and to test whether exposure translates into clinically meaningful outcomes. [X7]
